about: Pregnancy and breastfeeding reference for common foods and over-the-counter medicines. Written for a US audience: US sources (FDA, CDC, MotherToBaby) come first and the NHS page is kept as a second source. ACOG pages were not reachable, so ACOG is not cited. Educational only: it never says something is safe for a particular person, gives no doses, and sends every medicine question to a pharmacist or clinician. Texts are our own plain-language lines from the cited pages, each opened on its checkedAt date. Fish and fridge advice also has lessons in nutrition_paths.json; entries link there with learn.

pregnancy.why: The CDC says to avoid soft cheese made from raw milk, such as queso fresco, and to choose pasteurized versions, heated until steaming hot. Pasteurized feta, mozzarella and cream cheese are generally considered OK; the NHS adds that mold-ripened and blue cheeses are best cooked.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS says you do not need a special diet while breastfeeding, and the CDC says women generally do not need to limit or avoid specific foods. The pregnancy warning about soft and mould-ripened cheese is about listeria in pregnancy. Pasteurized cheese is still the everyday choice.

pregnancy.why: The CDC and FDA say to avoid raw milk and products made from it, which can carry listeria that is especially harmful in pregnancy. Pasteurized versions are the usual choice.

breastfeeding.why: The CDC says raw milk can carry germs that cause serious illness, and recommends pasteurized milk and dairy. That is general food safety, not something particular to breastfeeding.

pregnancy.why: The CDC and FDA say to cook eggs until the yolks and whites are firm, and to use pasteurized eggs for dishes with raw egg like mousse, tiramisu or homemade mayonnaise. Store-bought mayonnaise and dressings use pasteurized eggs. The risk is salmonella food poisoning.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS says you do not need a special diet while breastfeeding, and the CDC says women generally do not need to limit or avoid specific foods. The NHS pregnancy page notes that raw or runny eggs can still give you food poisoning, so cooking them through is the easier path.

entries.name: Deli meat, hot dogs and pâté

pregnancy.why: The CDC says to avoid deli meat and hot dogs unless they are heated to 165°F or steaming hot, because ready-to-eat meats can carry listeria. The NHS also asks for refrigerated pâté to be eaten before its use-by date.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS says you do not need a special diet while breastfeeding, and the CDC says women generally do not need to limit or avoid specific foods. The CDC advises reheating deli meat until steaming hot for higher-risk groups such as pregnant women and newborns; it does not name breastfeeding mothers.

pregnancy.why: The NHS says to avoid liver because it is very high in vitamin A, and too much vitamin A can harm the baby.

breastfeeding.why: Liver is very rich in vitamin A. The NHS says adults should not eat liver or liver products such as pate more than once a week; its page does not single out breastfeeding.

pregnancy.why: Fish is generally considered a good food in pregnancy. The FDA and EPA put salmon, shrimp, cod, sardines, canned light tuna and many others on a Best Choices list, with 2 to 3 servings a week.

breastfeeding.why: The CDC points to the same FDA and EPA lists while breastfeeding, since mercury can pass into milk.

pregnancy.why: Tuna has more mercury than most fish. In the FDA list canned light tuna is a Best Choice; albacore and yellowfin are a Good Choice, one serving a week; bigeye is on the avoid list.

breastfeeding.why: The same FDA and EPA lists apply while breastfeeding.

entries.name: Shark, swordfish, marlin and other high-mercury fish

pregnancy.why: These fish have the most mercury, which can affect a baby's developing brain and nervous system. The FDA and EPA list shark, swordfish, marlin, king mackerel, orange roughy, bigeye tuna and Gulf of Mexico tilefish to avoid.

breastfeeding.why: Mercury can pass into breast milk, so the CDC says to avoid the same fish while breastfeeding.

pregnancy.why: The CDC says to avoid raw or undercooked fish and shellfish, including sushi, sashimi and ceviche. Rolls made with cooked fish or only vegetables are generally considered OK.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS suggests no more than 2 portions of oily fish a week and no more than 1 of shark, swordfish or marlin while breastfeeding. Raw fish can also cause ordinary food poisoning, so choose a trusted place.

pregnancy.why: The CDC says to avoid raw or undercooked shellfish, which can carry bacteria or toxins. Refrigerated smoked seafood is also to be avoided unless it is in a cooked dish; shelf-stable sealed packs are the usual choice.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS says raw shellfish can contain bacteria or toxins that cause food poisoning. Its breastfeeding page sets no shellfish rule, so this is ordinary food safety: cooked is the lower-risk way.

pregnancy.why: The CDC says to avoid raw or undercooked sprouts such as alfalfa and bean sprouts; sprouts cooked until steaming hot are the usual choice. Keep cut melon refrigerated.

breastfeeding.why: The CDC lists sprouts among foods to cook until steaming hot for higher-risk groups, which include pregnant women and newborns. Breastfeeding mothers are not named, but cooking them is the lower-risk way.

pregnancy.why: The NHS suggests keeping caffeine to about 200 mg a day, roughly one 12 ounce cup of coffee, because more is linked to a higher chance of miscarriage and stillbirth. Tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate count too.

breastfeeding.why: Caffeine reaches breast milk in small amounts. The CDC says about 300 mg a day or less usually does not harm a baby; very high intake can leave a baby fussy and awake, and younger newborns clear it more slowly.

pregnancy.why: There is little research on herbal teas in pregnancy, so the NHS suggests no more than 4 cups a day and avoiding licorice root tea, which may harm the baby's development.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS suggests herbal teas as a swap for caffeinated drinks while breastfeeding. MotherToBaby says there is little information on herbal products and breastfeeding, so read the label and ask about any blend with added herbs.

pregnancy.why: The CDC says there is no known safe amount of alcohol and no safe time to drink during pregnancy. The NHS gives the same advice.

breastfeeding.why: The CDC says not drinking is the safest choice. Up to one drink a day is not known to harm a baby, and the usual advice is to wait about 2 hours per drink before feeding. Pumping and discarding does not clear alcohol faster.

pregnancy.why: Usually the first choice for pain or fever in pregnancy. MotherToBaby says to use it only as needed unless your OB or midwife advises otherwise; the NHS and the UK medicines regulator also say it remains safe to take.

breastfeeding.why: The NHS says paracetamol is usually the best painkiller while breastfeeding.

pregnancy.why: MotherToBaby, quoting the FDA, says NSAIDs are not advised after week 20 unless your OB or midwife recommends one, as they can affect the baby's kidneys and heart circulation. The NHS likewise says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it.

breastfeeding.why: Only small amounts reach breast milk, and MotherToBaby does not expect side effects in breastfed babies at usual use. The NHS says acetaminophen is usually the first choice. Check first.

pregnancy.why: MotherToBaby says many cold medicines are not expected to raise risks with short-term use, but some are preferred over others, and combination products mix several ingredients. Flu in pregnancy can be serious, so call your OB or midwife early.

breastfeeding.why: The same ingredient-by-ingredient question applies while breastfeeding.

pregnancy.why: MotherToBaby does not expect loratadine to raise the chance of birth defects, and the NHS also says it is generally considered OK in pregnancy. We did not open a source on other antihistamines, so ask about those.

breastfeeding.why: MotherToBaby lists loratadine as a preferred antihistamine while breastfeeding, and the NHS calls it one of the best choices. Tell your baby's pediatrician if the baby seems unusually sleepy; it may lower milk supply.

pregnancy.why: Antacids and alginates are commonly used for heartburn, but the NHS says some are not suitable in pregnancy, so tell the pharmacist you are pregnant. They can stop iron and folic acid being absorbed, so keep them apart.

breastfeeding.why: For Gaviscon, the NHS says it can be taken while breastfeeding and should not cause side effects in your baby. Other antacid brands have different ingredients, so check with your pharmacist.

pregnancy.why: MotherToBaby says mild steroid creams are often a first choice for skin problems in pregnancy: little reaches the baby through the skin, especially with small, short use on unbroken skin. Stronger creams and large areas are a different question.

breastfeeding.why: Typical use is not expected to affect a breastfed baby. If you use it on the breast, wipe it off before feeding.

pregnancy.why: The NHS warns that natural does not mean safe in pregnancy. Tell your OB, midwife or pharmacist about any herbal, homeopathic or aromatherapy product you use.

breastfeeding.why: MotherToBaby says there is little information on herbal products while breastfeeding, many have not been studied, and some have caused dangerous side effects. Products are not held to standards for ingredients or strength, so go through the label with your pharmacist or clinician.
